Discovery When Synthesis Is Cheap but Evidence Isn't

If a model can summarise fifty interviews in a minute, do you still need to run fifty interviews? The answer is neither yes nor no, and the useful form of the question is: which of the three costs of discovery actually fell?

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On 12 March 2026, Devesh Raikar sat in a glass room on the fourth floor of Pattri Freight Systems in Kharadi, Pune, with a printed synthesis in front of him and sixty-three enterprise logos on the wall behind him. Pattri sold transport-management software — dispatch planning, freight billing, e-way bill reconciliation, carrier settlement — to manufacturers and third-party logistics firms. Annual recurring revenue was ₹96 crore. The FY27 engineering plan committed ₹11 crore, a little over a third of build capacity, to a single bet called the Exception Console: a workspace for dispatch planners to handle the shipments that go wrong.

The case for the Console rested on a document Pattri's research lead, Farida Qureshi, had produced in nine days. A long-context model had read 4,100 support tickets from the previous three quarters, 1,240 recorded sales and renewal calls, and every implementation retrospective Pattri had ever filed. It found eleven recurring problem clusters. The largest, present in 38 per cent of tickets, described planners spending their mornings chasing exceptions across four screens. Nine months earlier that document would have taken a quarter and would not have been written. Devesh had asked for one number and could not get it: in eighteen months, Pattri's product team had spoken to nine dispatch planners. Nine, out of a population of roughly 2,800 across the customer base, because every conversation had to be cleared by the account manager who owned the relationship, and account managers were paid on renewal, not on research.

Three days earlier and 1,400 kilometres north, Ira Bhattacharya had faced a different version of the same problem. Ira ran the buyer experience at Jhalak, a live-commerce app in Gurugram with 14 million monthly actives, where small apparel businesses from Surat, Tiruppur and Ludhiana sold through short video. Jhalak's Navratri and Diwali planning locked on 20 March. The item under contention was Fit Confidence, a size-recommendation feature costing ₹6.8 crore to build and an estimated ₹1.1 crore a year to keep alive. Her growth team had synthesised 340,000 app-store and in-app reviews and 51,000 support chats; the model reported that fit and sizing were the single largest driver of dissatisfaction, named in 44 per cent of return-related conversations. They had also built a panel of eight synthetic buyer personas from the same corpus and had been running feature concepts past them in design reviews for two months.

Ira had spent the previous Thursday and Friday in a tailoring unit near Varachha Road in Surat, watching a seller named Bhavesh Rathod cut and pack. What she saw there did not appear anywhere in 391,000 documents, and it was the reason she was about to argue against a feature her own evidence appeared to support.

2. The idea, and the three schools that disagree about it

Discovery is the set of activities by which a team creates evidence about what customers need, as opposed to delivery, which builds things. It decomposes into three costs that are usually bundled and should not be. Sampling is access: identifying, qualifying, reaching and persuading the right people. Elicitation is extracting truthful information once you have them — the interview, the observation, the diary study, the shop visit. Synthesis is making sense of what was collected: reading, coding, clustering, writing the memo that a roadmap can be argued from.

The intellectual apparatus of product discovery was built when synthesis was the binding constraint. Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss gave the field theoretical saturation in The Discovery of Grounded Theory (1967): keep collecting until new cases stop producing new categories. Tom Landauer and Jakob Nielsen formalised the arithmetic in 1993 with the model that made "five users" famous — the proportion of problems found after n sessions is 1 − (1 − L)n, where L is the probability that any one session surfaces any one problem. Greg Guest, Arwen Bunce and Laura Johnson tested saturation empirically in 2006 and reported that twelve interviews produced most of the codes in their corpus. Steve Blank's customer development (2005), Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013) and Teresa Torres's continuous discovery (2021) are all, read economically, techniques for maximising the return on a small and expensive number of conversations.

Between 2023 and 2025, models with long context windows and good summarisation collapsed the third cost by roughly two orders of magnitude and left the first two almost untouched. Recruiting a dispatch planner at a Tata Motors supplier still takes a phone call, an account manager's permission and two weeks. Sitting with Bhavesh Rathod in Surat still takes a flight. Reading 391,000 documents now takes an afternoon and a few thousand rupees.

What practitioners disagree about is what follows from that. Three positions are held by serious people, and the disagreement is not semantic.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the parts nobody writes down

Expert practice has a shape. Seven steps, of which two are almost never written down and are the ones that matter.

Step one: inventory the corpora. Most companies over five years old hold evidence they have never read — tickets, call recordings, NPS verbatims, reviews, field-service notes, the customer-success Slack channel. Pattri held 21,900 documents. Jhalak held 393,000.

Step two, the first implicit one: write the provenance ledger. For each corpus, one sentence on why a document comes to exist, and one on what the selection rule excludes. A support ticket exists because someone was blocked and knew where to complain. A sales-call recording exists because a person carrying a quota chose to record a conversation with the economic buyer. Neither is a sample of your users; each is a sample of a mood, filtered through a channel, at a moment. Ten minutes per corpus, and every subsequent frequency reads differently.

Step three: synthesise adversarially, in at least three passes. The default pass finds themes. A second pass must ask for the outliers — "list the twenty documents least like the rest of the corpus and say why" — because summarisation is by construction a search for the modal case and the insight is frequently the exception. A third pass must ask, for each theme, "what would have to be observed for this to be false, and who would be in a position to observe it?" That third pass converts a report into a research plan.

Step four, the second implicit one: take the census of the missing. Enumerate the roles and segments that cannot appear in any corpus you hold. At Pattri the list was short and damning: dispatch planners appeared only indirectly, because tickets were raised by the customer's IT helpdesk on the planner's behalf; every planner who had left a customer; every prospect who had chosen FreightTiger or an in-house build; and the operations staff at the four accounts onboarded since October, too new to have generated tickets. That list is the recruiting brief. Most teams write the recruiting brief from the synthesis instead, which guarantees that the human round can only confirm what the corpus already contained.

Step five: allocate the interview budget by stratum, not at random. This is where the arithmetic earns its place, and it is worth doing explicitly.

The coverage formula is the Landauer–Nielsen one: the chance of hearing at least once about a phenomenon present in a proportion p of the population, over n conversations, is 1 − (1 − p)n. For p = 0.20 and n = 12 that is 1 − 0.812 = 0.931. For p = 0.05 and n = 12 it is 1 − 0.9512 = 0.460. The famous "twelve is enough" result holds for common phenomena in a homogeneous population and for nothing else. The two clauses are where most of the practical error lives.

Heterogeneity is the killer. If the thing you need to learn about lives in a stratum that is 15 per cent of the population, a random sample must be 10 ÷ 0.15 = 67 people to yield ten observations inside it. A stratified sample needs ten. The most valuable property of cheap synthesis is not that it answers questions; it is that it tells you which stratum the question lives in, and therefore converts a sixty-seven-interview study into a ten-interview one.

Step six: write the interview guide before reading the synthesis, and have it written by whoever will conduct the interviews. This sounds fussy and is not. A guide composed after reading a confident nine-page memo will contain the memo's categories, its vocabulary and its assumptions; the round then measures the corpus against itself. Step seven: keep a ledger in which every roadmap item names a claim, an evidence class and a human being.

Three second-order effects deserve naming, because they are where teams are actually being caught out. First, as synthesis approaches free, the number of questions a team can ask rises far faster than its capacity to adjudicate answers; the bottleneck migrates from analysis to judgement, which is what Figure 1 shows. Second, because transcripts are now valuable, organisations start recording everything, which raises real consent questions under the DPDP Act — purpose limitation means the grievance data you collected to resolve grievances is not automatically available as research material. Third, the research function's centre of gravity shifts from analysis, which is now cheap, to sampling design and question design, which are not, and which most research teams were not staffed for.

4. When it applies and when it is actively misleading

Four conditions, stated as claims you can test on a Tuesday rather than as principles.

C1: the corpus contains members of the population whose behaviour the decision will change. For Jhalak's buyer decision this passes overwhelmingly — buyers write reviews. For Pattri it fails: dispatch planners are the users, but tickets are raised by their IT helpdesk, so what the corpus holds is the helpdesk's paraphrase of a planner's frustration, two translations removed. Devesh's 38-per-cent cluster was therefore not a measurement of planners at all.

C2: the instrument that generated the corpus was not optimised against a different objective. Support tickets are optimised for closure; agents are measured on resolution time, so tickets record the shape that closes fastest. Sales calls are optimised for advancing a deal. Both are answers to questions nobody asked.

C3: the decision concerns an existing behaviour rather than a hypothetical one. Corpora describe the world as it is. Fit Confidence did not exist; nothing in 391,000 documents could say whether buyers would trust a size recommendation, and Ira's team briefly forgot that the volume of evidence about the problem said nothing about the solution.

C4: prevalence, not intensity, is the quantity the decision needs. If you need to know how many people are affected, counting utterances is defensible. If you need to know how much it costs them, it is not: articulacy and channel access determine who writes, and the most expensive problems are often the ones customers have stopped bothering to mention.

There is a fifth situation in which large-corpus synthesis is not merely weak but actively misleading: when the corpus is endogenous to the workflow you propose to change. If your last release created a reconciliation step, the tickets about that step will dominate the next synthesis, and the model will faithfully report that your customers' largest problem is the one you recently manufactured. The corpus is a mirror with a lag.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product companies hold corpora organised by product, because support queues are. The cross-product journey — the planner who moves from Pattri's dispatch module to its billing module and loses context — appears in neither queue's corpus, because the customer does not know which product to complain about. Machine synthesis over each corpus separately reproduces the org chart rather than the journey.

Two-sided businesses have the asymmetry Ira ran into.

Regulated products face an inversion that surprises people: the largest and richest corpus is often the least usable. Grievance records at a lender sit under a consent basis tied to grievance resolution; recorded advisory calls at a broker sit under SEBI record-keeping obligations. Under the DPDP Act, repurposing that material for product research is a question a data protection officer has to answer, not a product manager. Teams routinely discover this after the synthesis has been circulated.

Hardware-plus-software products defeat text corpora at the root. A two-wheeler's charging fault, a point-of-sale terminal's thermal behaviour in a Chennai summer, a wearable's strap failure — none of these are well described in words by the people experiencing them. The evidence is a photograph from a service centre and a technician's hands. A team that reads everything and visits nothing will build for the articulate subset of physical failures.

AI-native products have a closed-loop problem. If the product is a model and the synthesis of its failures is done by a model, the two share a family of blind spots: both will find the failures that are legible as language and both will smooth over the ones that are not. At minimum such teams need a human sampling pass over the raw logs, stratified on cases the evaluator scored as successes.

At the organisational seams, what mature companies say and do diverge sharply. They say research is democratised. What is usually true is that a small research-ops team spends most of its time on recruiting and scheduling — the expensive stage — while synthesis is done privately by individual PMs whose prompts nobody reviews. The quality control that used to be applied to analysis has not been reconstructed around sampling, which is now the part that determines the answer.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Frequency in a corpus is a channel artefact before it is a fact about customers

The tell-tale sign: theme rank correlates suspiciously well with which ticket categories have a mandatory free-text box. The obvious reading — that 38 per cent means 38 per cent of customers — is wrong because the denominator is documents, not people, and documents are produced by a process with its own incentives.

Saturation is a property of a segment, not of a study

The tell-tale: someone says "we reached saturation at twelve" without naming which population. Twelve conversations saturate a homogeneous stratum. Across four strata they are three apiece, which saturates nothing. The obvious reading treats a number from a 2006 paper as a constant of nature; it was a finding about one corpus of West African women's health interviews and does not transfer to a customer base with four business models in it.

Synthesis makes confirmation feel like discovery

The tell-tale: the memo contains no claim that makes anyone in the room uncomfortable. Models are trained to be helpful and tend to produce well-organised support for the framing implicit in the question. The obvious reading is that a clean result means a clear signal; the expert reads a frictionless synthesis as weak evidence that the question was leading.

Part of an interview's output is the interviewer

The tell-tale: a team with excellent research reports and poor instincts, usually one that outsourced interviewing to an agency. The obvious reading is that the transcript captures the interview. It captures the words. It does not capture the fourteen tabs open on the planner's screen, the fact that she keeps a paper register because she does not trust the system, or the pause before she answers.

Access is the real cost centre, and it is political rather than logistical

The tell-tale: the discovery plan has a "recruiting" line that has slipped three times and a "synthesis" line that never slips. Devesh's nine planners in eighteen months were not a research failure; they were a compensation-design consequence. The obvious reading treats recruiting as an operations problem for a junior person; the expert treats it as a negotiation with the revenue organisation and escalates it accordingly.

Endogenous corpora describe your own recent shipping

The tell-tale: the strongest theme in this quarter's synthesis is a problem introduced by last quarter's release. The obvious reading is that the team has found an urgent customer need; the expert first checks the theme's time series against the release calendar.

Synthetic personas are variance-reducers dressed as participants

The tell-tale: the persona never says "I don't know", never contradicts itself, and never has a reason that does not make sense. The obvious reading is that a persona is a cheap proxy for a customer. It is the opposite: it is a conditional mean over the corpus, and the variance it removes is precisely the variance you were sampling in order to observe. A persona can usefully carry known facts into a design review. It cannot be surprised, and surprise is the entire function of discovery.

Reading more raises hypotheses faster than it resolves them

The tell-tale: the candidate list grew from nine items to twenty-six and the team's conviction fell. The obvious reading is that more evidence should mean more certainty. In practice each additional corpus adds plausible claims at a rate that outstrips the team's capacity to test them, and the scarce resource becomes the willingness to close questions.

A quotation is not a verification

The tell-tale: the quoted line in the memo is real and the generalisation above it is not supported by that line. "It takes me all morning" supports a claim about one morning. Models attach the most vivid available quotation to a theme; the vividness does the persuading.

The absence of a theme is almost uninformative

The tell-tale: "nobody mentioned pricing" being read as "pricing is fine", in a corpus of support tickets where mentioning pricing would be pointless. Silence in a corpus is evidence about the channel, not about the world.

7. How this differs by product type and by stage

In consumer products the corpus is vast and shallow, recruiting is cheap, and the binding constraint is willingness rather than access. The risk is complacency: abundance makes ten conversations feel redundant when they are the only source of depth. In B2B and enterprise the corpus is small and heavily incentive-distorted, the population is countable, and access is gated by the revenue organisation. Here synthesis adds least and the organisational fight over access matters most. In platforms and marketplaces the defining fact is Figure 2: the corpus over-represents the paying side while the mechanism frequently sits on the other. In hardware, text is the wrong medium for the evidence. In AI products, the evaluator and the product share failure modes.

By stage, the difference runs opposite to intuition. A twelve-person company has no corpus; synthesis has nothing to chew on and there is no substitute for the first twenty conversations. A company of Pattri's size has both a large corpus and a rusted access path, which makes cheap synthesis simultaneously its biggest unlock and its most comfortable excuse. A company of Jhalak's scale has so much buyer evidence that the seller side becomes structurally invisible.

Where it is not different, and it is worth saying plainly: the census of the missing is identical work in every one of these settings, and so is the discipline of writing the guide before reading the synthesis. The difference is which names end up on the list, not whether the list is needed.

8. Three worked examples

Example 1: Devesh, and the value of an eighteen-interview round

Treat the decision as a wager. Committing ₹11 crore to the Exception Console returns an estimated ₹34 crore in three-year risk-adjusted value if the bet is right, and ₹3 crore of salvage if it is wrong. Farida's synthesis puts the probability it is right at 0.6. The alternative — splitting capacity across three smaller bets — is worth a steadier ₹7.5 crore.

Expected value of committing without further evidence: (0.6 × 34) + (0.4 × 3) − 11 = 20.4 + 1.2 − 11 = ₹10.6 crore. That already beats the split, so on the prior Devesh should commit and skip the interviews.

Now price the information. Suppose eighteen interviews with the right people classify the bet correctly 80 per cent of the time in each direction. If the round comes back positive, the posterior is (0.6 × 0.8) ÷ [(0.6 × 0.8) + (0.4 × 0.2)] = 0.48 ÷ 0.56 = 0.857, and the probability of a positive signal is 0.56. Expected value of committing after a positive: (0.857 × 34) + (0.143 × 3) − 11 = ₹18.57 crore. If negative, the posterior is (0.6 × 0.2) ÷ [(0.6 × 0.2) + (0.4 × 0.8)] = 0.12 ÷ 0.44 = 0.273, giving (0.273 × 34) + (0.727 × 3) − 11 = ₹0.45 crore — so he would take the split at ₹7.5 crore instead. Expected value with the round: (0.56 × 18.57) + (0.44 × 7.5) = 10.40 + 3.30 = ₹13.7 crore. The round is worth ₹3.1 crore. It costs about ₹53 lakh, counting incentives, team time and five weeks of deferred revenue. Run it.

Now change one input, and only one. Suppose the eighteen interviews are with the people Pattri can actually get to — IT managers and procurement contacts rather than planners — so the signal is right only 60 per cent of the time. Positive posterior: 0.36 ÷ 0.52 = 0.692, giving ₹13.45 crore; negative posterior: 0.24 ÷ 0.48 = 0.50, giving ₹7.5 crore, equal to the split. Expected value with the round: (0.52 × 13.45) + (0.48 × 7.5) = 6.99 + 3.60 = ₹10.6 crore — identical to deciding with no research at all. A round with the wrong participants has a value of information of approximately zero, and no increase in n repairs it. This is the single most useful number on this page.

Example 2: Ira, and the ceiling on Fit Confidence

Jhalak ships about 1.1 crore orders a quarter at an average order value of ₹640, so quarterly GMV is roughly ₹704 crore. The return rate on apparel is 31 per cent, giving 34.1 lakh returns; at ₹95 of reverse-logistics and handling cost each, that is ₹32.4 crore a quarter. Fit and sizing are named in 44 per cent of return conversations, so the addressable pool looks like ₹14.3 crore a quarter, against a ₹6.8 crore build. On the corpus alone, Fit Confidence is obviously worth doing.

Ira's fourteen seller visits changed one input. Of fit-related returns, roughly 65 per cent traced to label variance at source — the same nominal "M" differing by up to 1.5 inches between fabric lots, because sellers cut to the lot rather than to a standard. A recommendation engine trained on buyer data cannot fix a ground truth that moves. The addressable pool therefore falls to 35 per cent of ₹14.3 crore, or ₹5.0 crore a quarter, and only if the feature works perfectly. At a realistic 40 per cent effectiveness the annual benefit is about ₹8 crore against ₹6.8 crore of build and ₹1.1 crore a year of upkeep — a marginal bet rather than an obvious one. The alternative she took to the planning meeting was a seller-side measurement standard with a physical size-check kit, which no amount of reading would ever have proposed.

Example 3: Mahua Finserve, where the approach failed

In early 2025 Mahua Finserve, a Chennai-based lender to small businesses, synthesised 90,000 collections call transcripts and found a dominant theme: borrowers wanted to settle overdue instalments themselves, in the app, without speaking to an agent. It was a clean finding across a large corpus and the team skipped the interview round entirely. Self-serve settlement shipped in June 2025 at a cost of ₹4.2 crore. Four months later, adoption stood at 2.6 per cent against 22 per cent modelled.

The failure was endogenous selection, and it is obvious in hindsight. The corpus consisted of calls that reached an agent. Borrowers capable and willing to self-serve did not call; they were, definitionally, absent from every one of the 90,000 documents. The theme was real and its population was empty. The recovery took six weeks and twenty-two interviews plus nine ride-alongs with field collection officers in Nagpur and Indore. What emerged was that borrowers did not want privacy from the agent; they wanted a written confirmation on WhatsApp that they could show a spouse or a business partner. That feature cost ₹36 lakh and reached 19 per cent adoption in eight weeks. The cost of catching the error late was ₹4.2 crore and two quarters of the collections roadmap.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

"Twelve is enough; anything beyond it is theatre." The strongest form of this rests on real empirical work — Guest and colleagues found that twelve interviews yielded 92 per cent of their codes, and Nielsen's curve says the same thing in a different vocabulary. The position also has an economic argument: the marginal interview costs a fixed amount and returns a declining amount, so past some point the money belongs in delivery. For it to be wrong, it would have to be true that the decisions teams actually face hinge on low-prevalence or stratum-specific phenomena rather than common ones. In enterprise software, and in anything two-sided, that is usually exactly what is true.

"Synthesis at scale dominates interviews for prioritisation." Steelmanned: a synthesis over 21,900 documents covers phenomena an eighteen-interview round will never see, is reproducible, is auditable, and does not depend on the interviewing skill of whoever was free that week. Teams that adopted it found real problems they had been missing for years. For this to be wrong, the corpus would have to be selected in a way that correlates with the decision — which, as Mahua Finserve found, it frequently is — or the decision would have to concern something that does not yet exist.

"The value of contact is mostly transformational, not informational." This is the position with the weakest evidence and possibly the strongest claim. Its advocates argue that the function of sitting with Bhavesh Rathod is not the twelve facts Ira wrote down but the change in what she notices thereafter, and that this is why teams which stop degrade in ways that reading cannot arrest. For it to be wrong, it would have to be demonstrable that teams with no direct contact but excellent corpus practice make equally good calls over multiple cycles. Nobody has run that study, partly because the confound — teams that stop talking to customers usually have other problems — is very hard to remove.

"Synthetic participants will eventually be good enough." The honest version notes that models are increasingly able to reproduce known survey distributions, and argues that the objection is about current capability rather than principle. For it to be wrong, the transfer would have to fail specifically where it matters: reproducing a known distribution is a different task from anticipating a response to something that has never existed, and the failure is undetectable in advance because you have nothing to validate against. This one is genuinely open, and the practitioners who dismiss it entirely are as unserious as those who have already switched.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four observable ways. They read an unfamiliar synthesis by looking first at where the documents came from, not at what the themes say. They treat their interview budget as an allocation problem across strata rather than a number to be defended. They fight for access as a standing organisational arrangement — a quarterly commitment negotiated with the revenue leader, not a favour asked under deadline — because they know it is the stage the technology did not touch. And they keep asking the question that machine synthesis cannot answer and rarely prompts: who is not in this corpus, and does the decision depend on them? Someone who has merely studied the topic will say all of these things and will still, in March, build the recruiting list from the themes.

12. Closing: what each of them did

Devesh did not cancel the Exception Console and did not approve it. He took the ₹3.1 crore expected value of information to his CEO with the second calculation attached — the one showing that a round with the wrong participants is worth nothing — and used it to buy something he had failed to get for eighteen months: a standing agreement with Pattri's chief revenue officer that eight named accounts would provide two planner conversations a quarter, written into the account plan. Eighteen interviews ran between 18 March and 9 April. The Console survived, at ₹7 crore rather than ₹11 crore, with a scope change: the exceptions that mattered were not spread across four screens, they were spread across four people, and the problem was handoff, not navigation.

Ira killed Fit Confidence in its proposed form on 18 March and moved ₹2.4 crore of its budget to a seller measurement programme: a physical size-check kit, a standard chart, and a badge on listings from sellers who adopted it. She also retired the synthetic persona panel from design reviews, replacing it with a rule that any persona claim must be traceable to a conversation in the last ninety days. Her memo to the Jhalak leadership contained one sentence worth keeping: we had 391,000 documents about the symptom and none about the cause, and volume made that feel like knowledge.

Discussion questions.

1. Devesh's expected-value calculation says the research round is worth ₹3.1 crore with the right participants and nothing with the wrong ones. What would you have to believe about Pattri's account managers for the second figure to be the relevant one — and is that a research problem or a compensation problem?

2. Ira's seller visits overturned a conclusion drawn from 391,000 documents on the strength of fourteen observations. Under what conditions is that a triumph of fieldwork, and under what conditions is it a fourteen-person anecdote defeating a large sample? How would you tell the difference before the fact?

3. Mahua Finserve's corpus was large, real, and empty of the population the feature targeted. Design a standing check that would have caught this in week one rather than month four, and state what it would cost to run on every synthesis your team produces.

13. Going deeper

AI-assisted synthesis — the craft underneath step three: corpus preparation, adversarial prompting, outlier passes. It determines whether the input to every argument on this page is worth anything.

AI-assisted persona synthesis — the specific mechanism by which generated representations displace contact, and the conditions under which a persona is a legitimate carrier of known evidence rather than a substitute for evidence.

How AI is reshaping the PM role — discovery is the first place the shift bites, but the same asymmetry runs through specification, review and planning; this is the general form of the argument.

When building gets cheap and deciding does not — the delivery-side twin of this page, and the reason adjudication debt shows up in Figure 1.

The prototype as the new specification — the answer to condition C3: when the decision concerns a product that does not exist, a prototype is how you generate the evidence no corpus can hold.

What a PRD becomes when the reader can build — where the evidence ledger goes once the document's job changes from instruction to argument.

Reviewing work you did not write — the skill required to interrogate a synthesis you did not produce, which is now most of them.

Velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved — the general case of Figure 1: eliminating a stage rarely shortens the cycle by the length of the stage.

Taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill — once reading is free, deciding what is worth believing is the whole of the job.

Two lakh thirty-eight thousand documents say one thing. Twenty-one thousand vehicles say another. Fourteen home visits say a third. The board meets at nine.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

On the night of Sunday 4 October 2026, Shruti Iyengar sat at her dining table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with six documents open and a board deck that was still, at 10.20 p.m., missing its recommendation slide. Outside, the last of the Dussehra decorations were coming down from the gate of the apartment block opposite.

Shruti had been Chief Product Officer of Vaayu Mobility for nineteen months. On Monday morning she would ask the board to commit ₹38 crore — almost all of the company's discretionary capital for FY27 — to a programme called Vaayu Care. The papers had gone out on Thursday. On Friday evening, Devika Nambiar had sent her a spreadsheet from service operations that Shruti had not been able to stop reading, and on Saturday morning a survey result had landed that made a piece of the last two quarters' design work look like it had been done in a mirror.

The recommendation slide still said Approve Vaayu Care. Shruti was no longer sure the question on the slide was the right question.

2. How Vaayu got here, and the decision that still constrains it

Vaayu Mobility was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by two former automotive engineers and sold its first electric scooter, the Vaayu Sarj, in late 2020. By September 2026 it had a plant at Hosur, 42,300 cumulative units sold, an active fleet of about 39,000, FY26 revenue of ₹610 crore, and 118 dealer points concentrated in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Tamil Nadu. It was not the largest player and had never tried to be. Its position was reliability and service — the scooter that came back from the workshop the same day.

One decision from November 2022 shaped everything on Shruti's table. Faced with a choice between a swappable battery architecture and a fixed pack, Vaayu chose the fixed pack, with a proprietary connector, and signed a five-year supply agreement with Alkapuri Energy Cells of Vadodara. The agreement carried a minimum offtake of 55,000 packs over its remaining term with a ₹14 crore shortfall penalty, and the proprietary connector meant that any change to the pack's thermal design required new tooling and a fresh homologation cycle under AIS-156, the Indian battery safety standard introduced after the fires of 2022. The engineering team's estimate for a thermal redesign was ₹22 crore of tooling and nine months to re-certify through ICAT. In 2022 the fixed pack had looked like the cheaper, faster path. In 2026 it was the reason one of Shruti's three options took nine months.

3. The industry around them

The Indian electric two-wheeler market in 2026 was crowded and unsentimental. Ola Electric and TVS traded monthly registration leadership; Bajaj's Chetak had recovered strongly through its dealer network; Ather Energy had built the charging network and the enthusiast following; Hero's Vida and Greaves' Ampere fought at the value end. Every one of them sold on range. The certified figure on a Vaayu Sarj brochure, derived under the Indian Drive Cycle, was 128 km. Nobody in the industry believed a customer would see that number, and every manufacturer printed it.

Policy shaped the calendar. The PM E-DRIVE subsidy tranche Vaayu had qualified for was tied to registering 18,000 units by 31 March 2027; missing it cost roughly ₹7,200 a unit of effective price advantage in a segment where ₹5,000 moved share. GST on electric two-wheelers remained at 5 per cent. Telemetry from connected vehicles had become a live question under the DPDP Act: Vaayu's legal counsel had, in March 2024, insisted that location and usage telemetry be opt-in rather than opt-out, with the result that 54 per cent of the fleet transmitted and 46 per cent did not.

Vaayu's exposure was no longer only Indian. Karan Vora, who ran revenue from New Jersey, had spent the summer negotiating with Nasim Motors Trading, a Dubai distributor with reach across the northern Emirates. Nasim had put a letter of intent on the table for 6,000 units over eighteen months, worth about ₹74 crore, conditional on a written hot-climate range guarantee: a minimum usable range at 45°C ambient. The LOI expired on 15 November 2026.

4. The situation in detail

In February 2026 Tanuja Rao, Vaayu's head of data science in Toronto, brought a long-context synthesis pipeline into production. Every quarter it read the complete corpus of owner-generated text — 1,12,000 service records, 84,000 app reviews and in-app feedback entries, 31,000 call-centre transcripts and 11,400 dealer WhatsApp messages, 2,38,400 documents in all — and produced a ranked account of what owners were saying. It was the first time in Vaayu's history that anyone had read all of it. The February report was widely admired. The board asked for it as a standing item.

In April, Tanuja's team built Vaayu Voices: eight synthetic owner personas generated from the same corpus, which could be queried in design reviews. Lena Brandt, principal designer in Berlin, had used the panel in every review since May. It was quick, it was available at 3 p.m. Berlin time, and it never cancelled.

By July the picture looked settled. Range — specifically, the gap between the range the dashboard predicted and the range owners achieved — was the largest theme at 34 per cent of problem-mentioning documents. The conclusion drawn was that the range estimation algorithm and its presentation were the problem. Vaayu Care was scoped: a rebuilt range model using per-vehicle telemetry, a battery health report, predictive service scheduling, and a redesigned dashboard. ₹38 crore, fourteen weeks, shipping 12 November, in time for the festive tail and in time to give Karan something to write into the Nasim Motors guarantee.

Three things have since complicated it. In late September Prabhakar Menon, who runs the dealer network from Coimbatore, arranged nine ride-alongs and fourteen home visits on his own initiative, without a budget line, because his dealers in Nashik and Coimbatore kept telling him something that did not match the deck. On 30 September Devika Nambiar pulled service tickets per thousand vehicles by city and put them against the distance to the nearest Vaayu service point. And on 3 October, at Shruti's request, the research team ran a 310-respondent owner survey using five questions that had previously been put to the Vaayu Voices panel.

5. The people

Shruti Iyengar, Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru. Must present on Monday. Position: Vaayu Care is the right programme but she wants to know why the evidence keeps moving. Incentive: her credibility rests on the February decision to fund the synthesis pipeline, which she championed. Not saying: she has not personally spoken to an owner since March.

Rajat Bhandari, VP Engineering — powertrain and battery management, Pune. Position: the range gap is physical, not informational, and a software fix is a cosmetic answer to a thermal problem. Incentive: a pack redesign is his team's programme and his charter for two years. Not saying: the May thermal soak memo from Hosur, which showed pack derating above 42°C ambient, went to quality and was never pushed to product, and he did not chase it.

Tanuja Rao, Head of Data Science, Toronto. Position: the corpus is the most representative view of owners the company has ever had, and 2,38,400 documents should not be overturned by fourteen home visits. Incentive: the pipeline and the persona panel are her group's justification for a ₹6 crore platform budget in FY27. Not saying: 62 per cent of the corpus originates in four cities, and she has known this since the February build.

Karan Vora, Chief Revenue Officer, New Jersey. Position: ship Vaayu Care in November, close Nasim Motors, and solve the rest later. Incentive: exports are his growth story and his variable compensation. Not saying: in a call on 26 September he indicated to Nasim's principal that a hot-climate specification would be available by January, which is a commitment nobody in engineering has seen.

Lena Brandt, Principal Designer, Berlin. Position: the dashboard redesign is tested, the panel responses were consistent, and delay wastes two quarters of design work. Incentive: her team's output is the visible half of Vaayu Care. Not saying: she has never met a Vaayu owner outside a scheduled video call, and the persona panel has been her only source of owner reaction since May.

Meenakshi Sundaram, Head of Customer Experience, Singapore, covering the Gulf and South-East Asia desks. Position: the Gulf complaints are not about the app and never were. Incentive: her desk's first-contact resolution number is a board metric. Not saying: because there is no ticket category for heat-related range loss, her agents have been logging those contacts under "app connectivity", which both distorts the corpus and flatters her resolution rate.

Prabhakar Menon, Head of Dealer Network, Coimbatore. Position: the problem is where people charge, not what the dashboard says, and dealers have been saying so for a year. Incentive: an accessory and installation programme carries dealer margin. Not saying: several of his dealers have been selling unbranded extension-cable kits to owners, which is outside warranty terms and which he has not reported.

Dr Anjali Fernandes, VP Quality and Homologation, Hosur. Position: any pack change is a nine-month re-certification and she will not sign a hot-climate guarantee without a test campaign. Incentive: she carries personal regulatory liability. Not saying: she has observed lot-to-lot variance in cell impedance from one Alkapuri batch and has raised it only verbally.

Read in sequence, the exhibits do not converge. Exhibit 2 says the dominant owner concern is the range display, and it says so on the largest body of evidence Vaayu has ever assembled. Exhibit 3 says the range shortfall is real and physical and that it is worst in Nashik, Coimbatore and Kochi — the three cities contributing 12 per cent of the corpus between them. Exhibit 4 offers a mechanism for that gap: owners who live far from a service point raise fewer tickets, and the cities that generate the documents are the cities where the scooter performs best. Exhibit 5 proposes a different cause entirely, on fourteen observations collected by people with a commercial interest in the answer, using a question order that put the range display in participants' minds before anyone looked at a socket. Exhibit 6 undermines the instrument that has stood in for owners in every design review since May, while also showing that on two of five questions it was almost exactly right.

7. Voices

"We have read every word every owner has written for a year. I am being asked to set that aside because a dealer in Coimbatore took someone's photograph of an extension cord. If fourteen visits can overturn two lakh documents, what was the point of any of this?"

Tanuja Rao, product review call, 1 October, 8.30 p.m. IST / 11.00 a.m. Toronto

"The pack derates above 42 degrees. I sent the soak data to quality in May. Nobody asked product, and I will be honest, I did not walk it over. But the number in your deck is a display problem and the number in my lab is a chemistry problem, and you cannot patch chemistry in fourteen weeks."

Rajat Bhandari, same call

"Please can we be practical. Nasim has the LOI on the table until the 15th of November. They are not asking for a thermal report, they are asking for a specification with a number on it. I am telling you now because I saw it in your Exhibit 2 at eleven per cent and I think some of that eleven per cent is mine."

Meenakshi Sundaram, message to Shruti, 3 October, 2.40 p.m. SGT

"Madam, in Nashik I am not selling range. I am selling 'where will you plug it in'. Every second customer asks. We started keeping extension kits behind the counter two years back. It is not in any report because who will write a ticket about a plug point?"

"I want to say clearly that the panel has been useful and that I have designed eleven screens against it. I also want to say that I have not spoken to an actual owner since the Bengaluru sessions in February, and that until Friday I did not know that most of them do not have a socket."

Lena Brandt, design review notes, 3 October, Berlin

"I cannot sign a 45-degree guarantee on the current pack. I can run a test campaign at ICAT but that is eleven weeks minimum and I will need the Alkapuri lot data, which I have been asking for since June."

Dr Anjali Fernandes, note to the board papers, 2 October

8. The options as Shruti sees them

Option A: approve Vaayu Care as scoped. ₹38 crore, shipping 12 November, the festive tail, the PM E-DRIVE tranche, and something to put in front of Nasim Motors. It addresses the single largest theme in the largest evidence base the company has. It also, if Rajat and Exhibit 3 are right, spends the year's capital making a more accurate prediction of a shortfall the company has not fixed — and Shruti has noticed that a more honest range display would print a smaller number on a scooter competing with Ather and TVS on exactly that number.

Option B: divert to the pack and charger programme. ₹28 crore, nine months, a defensible hot-climate specification in July 2027. It treats the physical cause. It misses the festive window, puts the subsidy tranche at risk, forfeits the Nasim LOI in its current form, and exposes the company to the Alkapuri offtake penalty if volumes fall. Dr Fernandes is the only person who can say whether nine months is a real number, and she has not yet seen the lot data.

Option C: spend six weeks in the field first. ₹3.2 crore for a proper study — stratified by city distance-band, including owners with no telemetry consent, conducted by researchers rather than dealers. It would resolve whether Exhibit 5's mechanism is real. It also means arriving at the board in mid-November with a decision rather than a programme, having spent the festive quarter deciding.

Shruti has written all three on a slide. What she has not written, and what has been sitting at the edge of her thinking since Friday, is that all three options are framed as a choice about what to build, and that the evidence in front of her is mostly evidence about who she has been listening to. Exhibit 4 is not a fact about service centres. Exhibit 6 is not a fact about personas. There is also a fourth thing nobody has costed: Prabhakar's dealers estimate that a bundled home-charging kit with a certified 16A socket and installation would cost about ₹9 crore to stand up across 118 dealer points, would carry dealer margin, could ship in ten weeks — and would give the board no software story and Karan no number for Dubai.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 9 a.m. on Monday 5 October and expects a capital recommendation, not a process update. FY27 discretionary capital is ₹41 crore in total, of which ₹38 crore is on Monday's slide. The Nasim Motors LOI expires on 15 November. The PM E-DRIVE tranche requires 18,000 registrations by 31 March 2027; Vaayu is at 9,400 with two festive months and a wedding season left. The Alkapuri agreement carries a ₹14 crore shortfall penalty against a 55,000-pack minimum. AIS-156 re-certification for any thermal change is nine months and cannot be compressed. Telemetry covers 54 per cent of the fleet and legal has advised that broadening collection requires a fresh consent flow under the DPDP Act, which is itself an eight-week product change. Vaayu's research function is two people, both of whom are currently supporting the Vaayu Care design track.

10. Questions for discussion

1. What, precisely, does Exhibit 2 measure? Write the sentence that should appear as a footnote on it before it is shown to a board.

2. Exhibits 3 and 4 can be read as confirming Exhibit 2 or as gutting it. Construct both readings, and identify the single additional piece of data that would separate them.

3. Exhibit 5 rests on fourteen observations gathered by people with a commercial interest and an interviewer who asked about the range display before looking at anything. Exhibit 2 rests on 2,38,400 documents that nobody chose. Which is the stronger evidence for the decision in front of Shruti, and on what grounds?

4. Six of the eight people in section 5 are withholding something material. For each, say how the thing withheld would change the reading of a specific exhibit — and design the meeting, forum or metric that would have surfaced it before 4 October rather than after.

5. Tanuja's challenge is the sharpest one in the case: if fourteen visits can overturn two lakh documents, what was the pipeline for? Answer her in terms she would accept, and then say what the pipeline should be used for instead of what it has been used for.

6. It is Monday morning. Shruti has fifteen minutes and one slide. What does she recommend, what does she ask the board to approve, and what does she tell them she does not yet know — given that she cannot ask for both the capital and the six weeks?

11. 11.40 p.m.

Shruti went back to the recommendation slide a little before midnight. The cursor sat after the words Approve Vaayu Care. She thought about the eleven of fourteen households in Nashik running a lead out of a first-floor window, and about the 62 per cent of the corpus that came from four cities with workshops in them, and about Lena's eleven screens, and about a number Karan had already said out loud in Dubai. She thought about Tanuja's question, which she still could not answer cleanly, and about the fact that the last time she had sat on a scooter with an owner was in Jayanagar in March, and that she could not now remember what that owner had told her.

At 11.40 she deleted the slide, and then, a minute later, undid it. The deck saved itself at 11.52. The board met in nine hours and twenty minutes.

Nidaan Health Labs: Three Weeks to Decide What to Believe

A synthesis of 149,000 customer documents arrived in four hours. The discovery plan it was meant to replace would have taken five weeks. The contract that pays for the feature belongs to a segment that appears in 4 per cent of the documents.

1. Monday morning, Gachibowli

At 8.15 on the morning of Monday 7 September 2026, Aparna Deshmukh opened her laptop in the Nidaan Health Labs office on the fourth floor of a glass building in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, and found two messages waiting. The first, timestamped 11.40 p.m. Toronto time, was from Aditi Bhargava and carried a twenty-two page attachment titled Report Comprehension: Synthesis of 149,000 customer documents. The second, timestamped 6.05 a.m. Singapore time, was from Wei-Ling Tan and said only: Safeer wants an answer on the January date by the 22nd. They have a meeting with another vendor on the 25th.

Aparna had until Tuesday 22 September to tell the board what Nidaan would build with ₹4.6 crore of engineering capacity in the third and fourth quarters, and to say whether the company could commit to a January delivery. Fifteen days (Exhibit 1). Her original plan, drawn in July, had allocated five weeks of those fifteen days' worth of calendar to discovery: forty interviews across Hyderabad, Pune, Lucknow and Kochi, plus ten ride-alongs with phlebotomists. The synthesis had arrived a month early and cost ₹11,000 in compute. The question in the room, put by Nidaan's founder and chief executive Harish Vaidyanathan in a one-line WhatsApp message at 7.50, was blunt: Aditi has read everything. What are forty interviews going to tell us that 149,000 documents didn't?

2. Nidaan Health Labs

Nidaan was founded in Hyderabad in 2019 to do one unglamorous thing well: send a trained phlebotomist to a customer's home, draw blood, get the sample to an accredited lab within the stability window, and return a report to a phone. By September 2026 it ran about 4.2 lakh home collections a quarter across eleven cities, worked with fourteen NABL-accredited partner labs, and booked roughly ₹78 crore of annual revenue. It sat in a crowded market. Dr Lal PathLabs and Thyrocare had national scale and brand recall; Redcliffe Labs had gone hard at price; Apollo 24|7 and Tata 1mg bundled diagnostics with pharmacy and teleconsultation. Nidaan's differentiation had always been operational — a 94 per cent on-time collection rate, and phlebotomists who were employees rather than aggregated gig workers.

Revenue came from four distinct places. Urban self-pay customers booked on the app. Corporate contracts supplied annual health check-ups for employers, billed per employee. Doctors referred patients directly, particularly in Pune and Kochi. And a growing set of bookings were made by adult children — frequently living in New Jersey, Toronto or Dubai — for elderly parents in India, a segment Sandeep Nair had been building from New Jersey for two years.

The feature under discussion was called Samajh, an in-app explanation layer that would read a lab report and describe what each marker meant in plain Hindi, Telugu or English, with an explicit line about what the customer should do next. Lena Hoffmann in Berlin had designed three versions of it. The medical logic was the hard part, and Dr Sarita Rane, Nidaan's medical advisor in Pune, had been careful in every meeting to distinguish explanation from interpretation.

3. What the synthesis said, and what Aparna could not stop looking at

Aditi's document was good work. It covered 96,000 support chats, 41,000 app-store and in-app reviews, and 12,000 free-text notes filed by phlebotomists after collections. It found nine recurring themes. The largest, appearing in 38 per cent of documents that mentioned a report at all, was that customers could not read their own results: they saw a table of numbers with reference ranges, several markers flagged in red, and no sense of whether to be worried. The second largest was that they took the report to a general physician purely to have it explained, which cost them a consultation fee and two days.

Aditi had been careful. Her document included frequency counts by city, a confidence note on each theme, and twelve verbatim quotations. It read like a research report because it was one.

What Aparna could not stop looking at was a table she had pulled herself on Sunday evening (Exhibit 2). Corporate contracts produced 44 per cent of Nidaan's revenue and 4 per cent of its support chats, because corporate customers did not contact Nidaan — they contacted their own HR department, and HR contacted Wei-Ling. Safeer Group, the Dubai facilities-management firm whose 9,000 mostly Indian-origin staff were covered by an annual check-up contract worth ₹3.2 crore over two years, had never generated a single support chat in Nidaan's system. Neither had the HR managers who bought on their behalf. Every word of evidence about them lived in Wei-Ling's email, which was not in the corpus.

4. The people

Aparna Deshmukh, VP Product, Hyderabad. Eight years at Nidaan-sized companies, two of them here. She must present on 22 September. She believes the synthesis is real and also that it is answering a question she did not ask.

Aditi Bhargava, Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Built the synthesis pipeline over four months and is, understandably, proud of it. Her stated position: "We have moved from reading nine interviews to reading a hundred and forty-nine thousand documents. If that does not change the decision process, what was it for?" Her team's charter for 2027 depends on the pipeline being used.

Wei-Ling Tan, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Owns the Safeer relationship and the three other corporate accounts in the Gulf. She wants the January date because Safeer's renewal cycle closes in February and a competitor is circling. Her position: "I can get you two hours with Safeer's HR head and I can get you into their staff accommodation block in Al Quoz over video. Nobody has ever asked me for that."

Dr Sarita Rane, Medical Advisor, Pune. A pathologist by training, part-time with Nidaan since 2021. She is the only person in the discussion who has read the literature on patient comprehension of laboratory results, and the only one worried about the line between explaining a number and advising on it. Her position: "Under the DPDP Act this is sensitive personal data, and under every professional norm I know, telling a person what their raised creatinine means is not explanation. I need to know who is going to read what we ship before I sign it off, not after."

6. The options

Option A: decide on the synthesis. Accept Aditi's document as the evidence base, lock Samajh's scope this week, commit to January, and sign Safeer. Upside: the ₹3.2 crore contract is secured, the team gets eleven extra working days of build, and the largest theme in the corpus is almost certainly a real problem for self-pay users. Cost: the feature is designed entirely from the voice of a segment that is not the one paying for it, nobody has asked a Safeer employee anything, and Dr Rane's clinical concern is unresolved when the scope is frozen.

Option B: run the full July plan. Forty interviews and ten ride-alongs across four cities, finishing 12 October. Upside: genuine coverage, including the rarer problems that a fourteen-person round will miss, and a result Dr Rane can build a clinical review on. Cost: the board decision slips three weeks, the January date goes, and Wei-Ling's assessment is that Safeer will hear a competitor's pitch on 25 September with nothing from Nidaan to compare it against.

Option C: run a small stratified round against the gaps. Fourteen conversations in eleven days, allocated deliberately: four Safeer employees and the Safeer HR head over video from Dubai, three HR buyers at Indian corporate accounts, three referring doctors in Pune and Kochi, three caregiver-bookers in New Jersey and Toronto arranged by Sandeep, and one phlebotomist ride-along in each of two cities. The synthesis is used not as the answer but as the source of the questions and the map of which groups are already covered. Upside: the board date and the January date both hold, and the evidence gap that Exhibit 2 shows is closed where it matters. Cost: fourteen conversations will not surface uncommon problems, the sample inside each stratum is three or four people, and the round produces no comfortable "n = 40" number to put on a slide.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What exactly did Aditi's synthesis measure, and what would you have to add to Exhibit 3 before you could say how much of Nidaan's customer base it represents?

2. Harish's question — "what will forty interviews tell us that 149,000 documents didn't?" — is a fair one. Answer it in his terms, with reference to the segments in Exhibit 2.

3. If Aparna takes Option C, how should she allocate fourteen conversations, and what would she be knowingly giving up by not running forty?

4. What should Aparna commit to Wei-Ling on 22 September about the January date, given that she will have spoken to four Safeer employees and no more?

8. A note for the learner

The lens this case is asking you to use is a decomposition. Discovery has three costs: sampling (getting access to the right people), elicitation (asking them good questions) and synthesis (making sense of what you collected). Machine synthesis collapsed the third one to near zero between 2023 and 2026. It did not touch the first two. Harish's question assumes that all three fell together, and it is that assumption, rather than his impatience, that a well-reasoned answer has to take apart.

Once you separate them, Exhibit 2 stops being a curiosity and becomes the centre of the case. Nidaan's corpus is enormous, real, and produced almost entirely by one segment, because the process that generates a support chat requires an app, a problem and a self-pay customer. Reading it more thoroughly cannot manufacture evidence about people the process excludes. That is the specific thing no amount of processing substitutes for: recruiting the right people. The second thing is elicitation — nothing in 149,000 documents can tell Aparna whether a Safeer welder would trust an explanation of his own creatinine reading delivered in an app, because that feature does not exist and no one has been asked.

A defensible path is Option C, and the reasoning runs in three steps. First, the synthesis has already done the work it is good at: it has told Aparna which strata the question lives in, which converts a forty-person random sample into a fourteen-person stratified one and buys back three weeks. Second, the round should be allocated by decision weight rather than population share — corporate customers are 4 per cent of the chats and 44 per cent of the revenue, and the Safeer contract is the money on the table, so they get the largest block of conversations even though the corpus says almost nothing about them. Third, the fourteen conversations must be designed to falsify the synthesis, not to confirm it: the guide should be written before the team re-reads Aditi's themes, and it should ask people to describe the last report they received rather than whether they would like an explanation feature.

What Option C gives up is real and should be stated to the board rather than hidden. Three or four people per stratum will surface common problems and miss uncommon ones. Aparna should therefore commit to January on a deliberately narrow scope — explanation of a fixed set of common markers, reviewed by Dr Rane, with an explicit "discuss with your doctor" boundary — and schedule the remaining twenty-six conversations from the July plan into the build quarter rather than cancelling them. The point is not that fourteen is the right number. It is that fourteen chosen by the machine's map of who is missing is worth more than forty chosen by a calendar in July, and both are worth more than zero.

Discovery When Synthesis Is Cheap but Evidence Isn't

The question this page answers: if a model can summarise fifty interviews in a minute, do you still need to run fifty interviews?

1. Forty minutes that cost six weeks

On the evening of 4 February 2026, Rukmini Shenoy stayed back in the Sunwai Systems office in Andheri East, Mumbai, to read a nine-page document a machine had written in forty minutes. Sunwai sold grievance-management software — the workflow a bank or an NBFC uses when a customer complains about a failed transaction or a wrongly levied charge, and the clock starts on the window before the matter can be escalated to the RBI Ombudsman. Eleven lenders used the platform; between them they logged about 62,000 grievances a month.

The nine pages were a synthesis of 2,340 grievance transcripts from the previous quarter. A junior PM, Aditya Rao, had exported them, stripped the identifying fields to stay on the right side of the DPDP Act, and asked a long-context model to find the recurring shapes. It returned nine themes with counts and quotations. Three of them Rukmini had never heard articulated before — including one that agents were re-asking customers for information already supplied in the app, because two systems did not share a case object.

The problem was the calendar. Sunwai's roadmap locked on 20 February, and behind it sat about ₹6.5 crore of engineering capacity. Rukmini's December discovery plan called for 45 interviews across four lenders: six weeks of elapsed time, roughly 120 hours of her team's attention, finishing in the third week of March. The nine pages had arrived a month early and cost about ₹9,000 in inference.

Her CEO's question, sent on WhatsApp at 9.40 that night, was the honest one: if the machine already read everything, why are we still planning to talk to forty-five people? It is the right question, and answered badly it produces a roadmap that is fluent, well-evidenced-looking and wrong.

2. The idea

Discovery is the set of activities by which a team creates evidence about what customers need, as distinct from delivery, which builds things. It has three cost components, and the whole argument turns on keeping them apart. Sampling is access: finding the right people, qualifying them, persuading them to give you time. Elicitation is getting truthful information from them once you have them. Synthesis is making sense of what you collected — reading, coding, finding patterns, writing the memo.

Until about 2023, synthesis was the binding constraint, and the field's apparatus grew up around that scarcity. Glaser and Strauss, introducing grounded theory in 1967, gave researchers theoretical saturation: stop collecting when new cases stop yielding new categories. Steve Blank's customer development (2005) and Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013) both optimise for a small number of high-quality conversations. Teresa Torres's continuous discovery (2021) spread a fixed synthesis budget across time.

Long-context language models collapsed the third cost to near zero and left the first two where they were. That asymmetry is the whole event. Discovery did not get cheaper; one of its three legs fell by two orders of magnitude and the others did not move.

The sentence Rukmini could say in a meeting without sounding glib: synthesis got cheap, sampling and elicitation did not — so read far more of the evidence you already own, and spend your scarce human hours on the people you have never spoken to.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics are not complicated, but two steps are almost always left implicit, and those are the steps that separate practitioners from people who own the vocabulary.

First, inventory the evidence you already own: grievance transcripts, support tickets, sales-call recordings, NPS verbatims, app-store reviews, implementation retrospectives. Before 2023 these went unread because reading them was a quarter of someone's job. Now they go unread only out of habit.

Second — the first implicit step — label each corpus with its provenance and its selection rule. A grievance transcript exists because a customer was upset enough to file. A sales-call transcript exists because a salesperson with a quota chose to record. None of these is a sample of your customers; each is a sample of a particular emotional state filtered through a particular channel. Writing that sentence down, per corpus, takes ten minutes and changes how every later number is read.

Third, run machine synthesis to generate hypotheses, not conclusions. The output is a list of candidate claims with candidate frequencies attached. Each needs a way of being wrong.

Fourth, and the second implicit step, take the census of the missing: write down who could not possibly appear in the corpus. For Sunwai that included every customer who gave up without filing, every agent who had quit, every compliance officer (who never touches the complaint form), and the three lenders live for under four months whose volumes were too small to register. That list is the recruiting brief.

Fifth, run a small, targeted human round: a few conversations to test the machine's hypotheses against someone who can contradict them, and a few with the people the corpus structurally excludes. Sixth, re-synthesise machine and human evidence together. Seventh, keep a decision log in which every roadmap item names both a theme and a person.

4. A worked example, with the arithmetic shown

Rukmini's real question was: how many interviews, with whom, and what does cutting cost? The useful arithmetic is old. If a problem is present in a proportion p of your population and you talk to n people drawn at random, the probability you hear about it at least once is 1 − (1 − p)n. That is the whole formula, and it is why the literature keeps landing on "about twelve interviews".

Take a common problem, present in 20 per cent of agents' working lives. With twelve interviews, 1 − (0.8)12 = 1 − 0.069 = 0.931. Now take a rare problem, present in 5 per cent: 1 − (0.95)12 = 1 − 0.540 = 0.460. You miss it more often than you catch it. To reach 90 per cent on the rare problem you need forty-five: 1 − (0.95)45 = 0.901. Rukmini's December plan had been sized — without anyone saying so — to catch 5 per cent problems.

Now change one input. Suppose the decision hangs not on agents in general but on a segment — the compliance officers at the three newly onboarded co-operative lenders, perhaps 15 per cent of the relevant population. To get ten conversations inside that segment by recruiting at random you need 10 ÷ 0.15 = 66.7, call it sixty-seven interviews. To get ten by recruiting deliberately you need ten. The number collapses by a factor of six the moment you stop sampling randomly and start sampling on purpose. That is the most useful consequence of the whole shift: because the machine has already told you which segment the question lives in, you can spend the interview budget stratified rather than scattered.

The marginal value of the first conversation with a compliance officer — a role appearing nowhere in any of those corpora — was very high, and no amount of processing could manufacture it.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Prevalence is not intensity, and the model counts mentions

When a synthesis says a theme appeared in 38 per cent of transcripts, it reports how often something was said, not how much it mattered. Verbose complainants, categories with a mandatory free-text field, and issues that are easy to articulate are all over-represented. Ask of every frequency: what would make someone mention this, and what would stop them?

A corpus of complaints is a census of complainers

Sunwai's 2,340 transcripts tell you a great deal about people who filed a grievance and nothing about the larger group who silently moved their salary account elsewhere. Volume makes selection bias feel less dangerous when it does the opposite: 2,340 biased observations read far more convincingly than twenty.

Synthesis quality is bounded by elicitation quality

A model summarises badly asked questions beautifully. If agents were trained to close the ticket rather than understand the problem, the transcripts record the closure. Machine synthesis cannot detect that the underlying instrument was blunt; it produces a confident, well-organised account of the blunt instrument's output.

The model regresses to the modal phrasing, and the outlier is often the insight

Summarisation works by finding what is common. The single furious transcript from a treasury manager at a Dubai client describing a workflow nobody else has is exactly the signal a summary is built to smooth away. Experienced teams ask for outliers as a separate pass: list the ten transcripts least like the others, and say why.

Fluency reads as evidence

A nine-page memo with headings, counts and quotations carries the social signature of a research report. It arrives with confidence it has not earned and is hard to argue with in a room, because arguing requires having read the underlying material and nobody has. The defence is procedural: whoever presents a machine theme must name one human being who confirmed it.

Generated personas cannot surprise you, by construction

A synthetic persona is an interpolation over evidence already in the corpus. It can restate what is there in a more usable voice, which is genuinely useful. It cannot contain what was never in the input, so consulting it in place of a person guarantees discovery returns only what you had. "We asked the persona" is evidence converted into an echo.

Talking to someone changes the researcher, not just the notes

Part of what an interview produces is tacit: the tone when an agent describes her fourteenth escalation of the shift, the nine tabs open on her screen. None of it survives into a transcript, so none survives into a synthesis. There is also an organisational function. "I sat with Sushma in the Pune service centre on Tuesday" carries weight that "theme four, 38 per cent" does not — and that weight is the room correctly discounting evidence nobody has touched.

What it cannot tell you however well you apply it

No corpus contains evidence about a product that does not yet exist. Grievance transcripts describe the current workflow; they cannot say whether agents would adopt a proposed one, whether a lender's procurement committee would pay, or what people do under a load they have never met. Those questions need a prototype or a price conversation, not more reading. So the newcomer's questions before relying on any synthesis are: what is in this corpus, who is structurally absent, who wrote the questions that produced it, and what observation would change the conclusion?

6. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the corpus is enormous and shallow. A payments app has millions of store reviews and support chats; synthesis over them is nearly free and genuinely informative about breadth. The danger is that abundance makes ten hard-won conversations feel unnecessary, when they are the only place depth lives. Recruiting is cheap here, so there is no excuse.

In B2B and enterprise the arithmetic inverts. There may be forty accounts in total, so a sample is a meaningful fraction of the universe. The available corpus is dominated by sales-call transcripts — the most incentive-distorted evidence in the building, recording what a quota-carrying person chose to record in a conversation with the buyer rather than the user. The scarce resource is access, because the account team owns the relationship and has every reason to protect it.

In marketplaces the structural fact is two sides and one voice: tickets and reviews almost always come from the side that pays. A delivery platform's corpus is thick with diner complaints and thin on rider experience, and the rider side is where the operationally surprising things are.

By stage, the difference often runs the opposite way to expectation. An eight-person startup has no corpus; synthesis has nothing to chew on and there is no substitute for twenty conversations. A large company has a vast corpus and a rusted access path — legal review, account-team gatekeeping, a rule against unapproved customer contact. For it, cheap synthesis is a real unlock and a real temptation, because it offers a way to look well-informed without fighting the access battle.

7. Common mistakes

The synthesis-only roadmap

The symptom from outside: every roadmap item traces to a theme name and none to a person's name. The misunderstanding is treating a summary as evidence rather than a compression of it. The diagnostic takes thirty seconds — point at the top item and ask, "name one customer, and tell me what they said." If the answer is a percentage, the item has never been checked.

Interviewing to confirm the machine

The symptom is a guide whose questions begin "we've found that… do you agree?" The misunderstanding is that the human round validates the synthesis, when it exists to falsify it. Count the questions: what share ask about a specific past event ("walk me through the last time you re-asked a customer for a document") versus an opinion about a future one? A guide more than a third opinion questions will confirm whatever it was given.

Volume theatre

The symptom is a slide reading "analysed 21,657 documents". The misunderstanding is that volume substitutes for relevance. One question catches it: what share of those documents came from the segment this decision affects? At Sunwai, for the co-operative-lender decision, the honest answer was close to zero.

Persona substitution

The symptom is a design review in which someone consults a generated persona instead of a customer and nobody finds it odd. Ask when the persona was last revised because a real conversation contradicted it. If the answer is never, it is not a research artefact; it is a mirror.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the same February looks like this. Aditya's synthesis runs over all 21,657 documents, because reading is free now, and runs three times: once for themes, once for outliers, once for "what question would test each theme with a human". Every theme enters a ledger with three columns — the claim, the evidence class behind it, the person who would know whether it is true. The team holds a standing floor of two customer conversations a week regardless of what is being decided, so access never has to be re-established under deadline. Before the interview list is drawn, someone writes the census of the missing and the list is built to cover it rather than to fill a number. And the guide is written by whoever will run the interviews before they read the synthesis, so the questions are not contaminated by the machine's framing.

9. What Rukmini decided

She cut forty-five to eighteen and changed who the eighteen were. Six were grievance agents at the two largest lenders, chosen to test the three novel themes and to try to break them. Six were compliance officers — a role with zero representation in any corpus Sunwai owned. Six were operations staff at the three new co-operative lenders, the segment the machine could not see. The round finished on 19 February, one day before the lock, and cost about ₹47,000 in incentives and thirty-eight hours of team time.

Two of the three novel themes survived contact. The third — a confident claim that agents wanted a bulk-resolution tool — died in the second interview, when an agent explained that bulk resolution was precisely what her team lead's audit rules forbade. It appeared in the transcripts because agents talked about wanting it; it never appeared that anyone could use it. Rukmini's decision log recorded one line: we used the machine to decide who to talk to, not to decide what to build.

What to learn next: AI-assisted synthesis, because what you get out depends on how the corpus is prepared and the question posed, and that is a craft with real technique; AI-assisted persona synthesis, because the failure above is the commonest in practice and worth seeing up close; and taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill, because once reading is free, deciding what is worth believing becomes the job.

Two questions to sit with.

1. Name the largest corpus your team owns and has never read. Who is structurally absent from it — and what decision are you making right now that depends on exactly those people?

2. If your next synthesis came back saying precisely what you already believed, how would you tell confirmation from an echo?
